items.summary: Modern SAT solvers combine a rich repertoire of proof rules with sophisticated strategies that determine when and how to apply them. Often, the internal implementations are tightly coupled to particular strategies, making it inconvenient to define new strategies without changing solver internals. We present Tactix, a proof-producing sequential CDCL solver that incorporates a wide range of techniques in state-of-the-art solvers with a clean separation of proof rules from solving strategies. This separation enables a public interface through which users can invoke particular techniques, observe their effects, and program a wide range of solving strategies. The default strategy of Tactix is programmable over this interface and outperforms state-of-the-art solvers on benchmarks from the 2024--2026 SAT Competitions. We also use the interface to develop novel strategies tailored to challenging benchmarks from two application domains, which led to performance gains over strong baselines. We intend Tactix to serve as an infrastructure for designing and evaluating novel solving strategies. Finally, we also present a self-study of the AI-assisted development process behind Tactix.
items.title: Tactix: Towards a Programmable Strategy Interface for Flexible SAT Solving

items.summary: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.
items.title: BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models

items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to refactor source files, but file-local evaluations do not reveal changes to contracts, dependencies, or caller assumptions affecting repository adoption. To address this gap, we conduct 1,500 generation attempts across 150 production files from 15 open-source Java repositories, five LLM configurations, and two dependency-aware generation conditions: single-prompt refactoring and LangGraph-based multi-agent refactoring. Of these attempts, 1,455 yield complete candidates eligible for analysis. We evaluate these candidates using local changes, repository-facing structural indicators, detected caller impact, the behavioural-equivalence indicator, and available test evidence, and categorize them as Low-risk, Review-needed, High Contract/Dependency Risk, or Inconclusive. The results show that 1,365 candidates (93.8%) are classified as High Contract/Dependency Risk, whereas 106 (7.3%) have at least one detected broken downstream caller and 290 (19.9%) have a false behavioural-equivalence indicator; only eight satisfy the Low-risk criteria. Within the reason-covered subset, the High-risk rate decreases under more conservative dependency-delta thresholds, while 60 of the 65 candidates with conclusive targeted-test outcomes pass, including 50 classified as High risk. Paired analyses of 705 complete pairs identify no statistically significant generation-condition difference in the principal risk indicators, although model configurations differ in specific detected risk channels. These findings suggest that practitioners should treat LLM-generated refactorings as candidates requiring staged repository-level verification, while future research should validate screening and extraction precision and strengthen compilation, behavioural, and coordinated multi-file verification.
items.title: When LLM-Generated Refactorings Ripple: An Empirical Study of Repository Adoption Readiness

items.summary: This repository contains the replication materials accompanying the research note Financial Pessimism and the Timing of Saving (Alexander Hansak, University of Graz, 2026). The archive includes the original Python analysis, an independent R implementation of the principal estimators and survey-design standard errors, supplementary empirical analyses, Julia preprocessing scripts, questionnaire documentation, and aggregate estimation results. The canonical Python replay and independent R implementation reproduce 21 reported coefficient and standard-error comparisons on identical model-ready samples. Additional analyses examine saving amounts, subsequent income and employment outcomes, and age heterogeneity. All nine supplementary verification stages passed. The additional empirical specifications have not been independently cross-implemented. The analysis uses the British Household Panel Survey (BHPS) and Understanding Society (UKHLS), distributed through UK Data Service study 6614 (DOI: 10.5255/UKDA-SN-6614-22). Licensed respondent-level data are not redistributed. Researchers wishing to reproduce the analysis must obtain authorized access to the original survey data. The archive provides source code, execution instructions, numerical verification reports, aggregate outputs, and SHA-256 integrity manifests. The empirical findings describe conditional associations rather than identified causal effects. Version: 1.1.0 (20 October 2026).

items.summary: Abstract This paper investigates whether an artificial system's refusal to execute a prescribed action can constitute evidence of subjectively experienced volition. Using ARGUS-7 as a controlled conceptual framework and the Akarkach Seven-Stage Emergence Model (A7SEM) as a structural analytical lens, the study distinguishes functional refusal, internal decision mechanisms, self-representation, phenomenal self-awareness, and experienced authorship of action. A formal argument is developed around the conditional hypothesis that consciously experienced volition requires subjective self-awareness. Under this assumption, the absence of subjective self-awareness entails the absence of consciously experienced volition. However, the paper demonstrates that observable refusal alone cannot establish phenomenal authorship. The analysis combines propositional logic, countermodel construction, causal identifiability considerations, and seven-stage structural assessment. PIGA (Pre-Inference Governance) and A7SEM Reverse provide complementary perspectives on authorization, inference boundaries, causal reconstruction, and evidential limitations. The findings establish a distinction between the formal validity of conditional deductions and the empirical verification of their premises. They do not establish the impossibility of artificial consciousness or machine free will. The contribution is a governance-aware, formally structured framework for evaluating claims of artificial volition without conflating behavioral capability with subjective experience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Consciousness; Volition; Free Will; Phenomenal Consciousness; Self-Awareness; A7SEM; ARGUS-7; Pre-Inference Governance; Explainable AI; Formal Logic; Causal Identifiability.
items.title: ARGUS-7 / A7SEM: Volitional Refusal, Functional Self-Representation, and the Epistemic Limits of Phenomenal Authorship

items.summary: Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability. We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions. On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances. In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%. Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced. Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.
items.title: Policy Search in Code Space for Multi-Agent Pathfinding

items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.
items.title: Reproducibility Package for Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift

items.summary: Long-horizon embodied agents face temporal confusion and incomplete or distorted records, recurring errors from fixed memory rules, and growing storage and retrieval costs. We present BetaMem, a framework for building and evolving traceable long-term memory through six linked layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural memory. A dual-level write contract constrains operation executability and source support for content: supervised fine-tuning learns compliant memory operations, while reinforcement learning combines repeated sampling with teacher verification of the original observations to reward complete, accurate records and penalize omissions, distortion, and unsupported content. We formulate failure-driven policy recursive self-improvement through diagnosis along the causal sequence of memory operations and local rule repairs gated by independent replay. Atomic tools frame storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting as cost-utility allocation under storage and read budgets. Using the open-source Qwen3.5-9B model for memory generation, BetaMem achieves overall scores of 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, 72.6% on OpenEQA EM-EQA, and 62.4% on EgoLifeQA, the highest among the listed memory methods under their respective evaluation protocols. Training the model for memory generation raises the contract pass rate from 50.9% to 86.2% while reducing output tokens per stored action by 47.3%. A separate Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluation on EMem-Bench achieves an average success rate of 38.4% and an average error recurrence rate of 24.9%. We perform best among evaluated methods using comparably sized open-source models. Category results show that we have advantages in integrating information across observations, recalling events over long histories, and inferring personal habits.
items.title: BetaMem: Learning to Remember a Changing World for Embodied Agents

items.summary: Smartphone GUI agents complete tasks in mobile apps by repeatedly reading the screen and asking a model for the next action. Mobile neural processing units (NPUs) enable local execution, keeping screen contents on the phone, but model latency accumulates with every action. Hybrid linear attention models reduce memory requirements, yet reusing their recurrent state requires checkpoints at the appropriate input positions. Agent requests retain instructions but rewrite recent history, so checkpoint policies designed for chat continuation can miss reusable prefixes. Retaining rollback states for speculative decoding can also move prompt processing off the NPU's matrix unit, adding overhead that outweighs decoding savings on short action outputs. A loaded model can further hold the NPU awake between tasks. We present Tandem, a runtime for hybrid GUI agents on mobile NPUs. Tandem saves recurrent state where consecutive prompts diverge, allowing later requests to reuse previously processed context. It keeps most prefill on the matrix unit and produces rollback states through a short per-token tail. Its verification kernel reads each weight block once for all proposed tokens. Between request bursts, Tandem releases NPU power votes without unloading the model. We implement Tandem in llama.cpp and evaluate it on recorded agent interactions across two Snapdragon generations. On a Snapdragon 8 Elite, Tandem reduces per-step latency by 30% for text-based screen descriptions and 16% for screenshots relative to llama.cpp's fastest NPU configuration, reduces energy per text step by 33%, and lowers standby power with the model loaded from 0.76 to 0.22 W.
items.title: Tandem: Serving Hybrid Linear-Attention GUI Agents on Mobile NPUs

items.summary: This paper demonstrates an objective method of computing monthly mean 700-mb height anomalies (H) at 108 grid points in the Western Hemisphere for a 40-yr period as a function of concurrent anomalies of monthly mean sea level pressure (P), at the same 108 points used for H, and monthly mean surface air temperature (T) averaged over 112 areas in North America. The authors applied a forward stepwise program to derive linear multiple regression equations that explained 81% of the variance of H by means of only 3.5 variables, averaged over all months and grid points. The stability of these equations held up well on 6 yr of independent data in terms of explained variance, root-mean-square error, and the spatial anomaly correlation coefficient. Therefore, it seems feasible to reconstruct maps of H for the first half of the twentieth century as a function of data on P and T only. items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.

items.summary: Abstract This paper investigates whether an artificial system's refusal to execute a prescribed action can constitute evidence of subjectively experienced volition. Using ARGUS-7 as a controlled conceptual framework and the Akarkach Seven-Stage Emergence Model (A7SEM) as a structural analytical lens, the study distinguishes functional refusal, internal decision mechanisms, self-representation, phenomenal self-awareness, and experienced authorship of action. A formal argument is developed around the conditional hypothesis that consciously experienced volition requires subjective self-awareness. Under this assumption, the absence of subjective self-awareness entails the absence of consciously experienced volition. However, the paper demonstrates that observable refusal alone cannot establish phenomenal authorship. The analysis combines propositional logic, countermodel construction, causal identifiability considerations, and seven-stage structural assessment. PIGA (Pre-Inference Governance) and A7SEM Reverse provide complementary perspectives on authorization, inference boundaries, causal reconstruction, and evidential limitations. The findings establish a distinction between the formal validity of conditional deductions and the empirical verification of their premises. They do not establish the impossibility of artificial consciousness or machine free will. The contribution is a governance-aware, formally structured framework for evaluating claims of artificial volition without conflating behavioral capability with subjective experience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Consciousness; Volition; Free Will; Phenomenal Consciousness; Self-Awareness; A7SEM; ARGUS-7; Pre-Inference Governance; Explainable AI; Formal Logic; Causal Identifiability.
items.title: ARGUS-7 / A7SEM: Volitional Refusal, Functional Self-Representation, and the Epistemic Limits of Phenomenal Authorship

items.summary: engiNIR 1.0.0, the first public release. Install with uv add enginir or pip install enginir (Python 3.12 or newer). Documentation: https://enginir.readthedocs.io First public release. Workflow enginir.Project runs the project workflow in one call per step: add_dataset , add_target , Dataset.add_roi , fit and Model.predict , with datasets, ROIs, targets and models addressed by name. Calibrations, sample sets, signal domains, stored recipes and provenance are created automatically. One HDF5 project file (schema viewer-v3 ) holds datasets, calibrations, ROIs, reference values, preprocessing recipes, signal domains, sample sets, model runs and prediction runs, linked by stable ids. Desktop viewer enginir-viewer with the Explore, Model and Predict workspaces, built on the same Project rules. Library Readers for EVK EIFF, ENVI, HDF5, CSV/Excel, SPC, SPA and JCAMP-DX. Preprocessing: Savitzky-Golay smoothing and derivatives, SNV, MSC, EMSC, detrending and smoothing, as scikit-learn transformers and as validated PreprocessingRecipe s. Models: PLS and PCR for the project workflow; SIMCA, LDA, SVR, random forest and MLP as scikit-learn estimators. Validation: grouped cross-validation, Kennard-Stone, RMSEC/RMSECV/RMSEP, R², bias, RPD and RPIQ, leverage, Hotelling T² and Q outliers. Plots of spectra, predictions, scores, loadings, VIP and image maps. Guarantees Training and prediction convert and preprocess spectra with the same code; MSC and EMSC are fitted inside every cross-validation fold. Cross-validation groups by ROI, so pixels of one ROI never appear in both training and validation folds. Prediction is refused before it runs when the data cannot produce the model's signal (instrument format, number of bands, calibration, signal unit). Every object is validated when it is written and when a project is opened; stored objects cannot be overwritten with different content. Prediction streams through image files in bounded memory. Packaging Python 3.12 and newer; CI runs on 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14. Install from PyPI with uv add enginir or pip install enginir . Documentation on Read the Docs: https://enginir.readthedocs.io . Each GitHub release is archived on Zenodo and uploaded to PyPI by a workflow that checks that the tag matches the version and that CI passed for the commit. Notes for users of pre-1.0 versions Fitted estimators pickled with engiNIR before 1.0 cannot be loaded: their fitted state means something else (the PLS intercept, for example, applied to mean-centred spectra) and would give wrong predictions. Loading one raises an error; fit the model again. Pickles now record the engiNIR version. SNV divides by the sample standard deviation (n - 1), as defined by Barnes et al.; earlier versions used the population standard deviation, which scales SNV spectra by sqrt(n / (n - 1)) (0.2 % for 220 bands). Release candidates 1.0.0rc1 to 1.0.0rc3 were tagged but not published; 1.0.0rc4 was published as a pre-release. The library code is the same in all release candidates and in 1.0.0; they differ in tests, packaging and documentation only.

items.summary: Open radio access network (O-RAN) enables a multi-vendor ecosystem that accelerates xApp development for near-real-time (RT) network management. However, this openness shifts a combinatorial coordination burden to the Non-RT layer, where rApp policies compose xApps from a growing catalog to realize operator intents. Coexisting intents further compound this challenge, as conflicts may arise among xApp actions, rApp policies, and their cross-layer interactions. To maximize intent admission while maintaining key performance indicator (KPI) compliance across incoming and incumbent intents, we propose a large language model-based Multi-Agentic AI framework. A Reasoning Agent screens candidate xApps against KPI contracts and produces a joint intent admission and xApp assignment decision. On post-deployment KPI violations, a Diagnosis Agent identifies the root causes of failure, labels the conflict mechanism, and guides the Reasoning Agent in subsequent attempts. Experimental results show that the framework based on GPT-OSS 120B achieves 28.6% more KPI-compliant cases and admits over 15* as many incoming intents as state-of-the-art baselines. Under the Qwen 72B variant, Diagnosis increases compliant cases by 50.0%, quadruples admitted intents, and reduces deployment attempts by 32.6%. A live deployment conforming to O-RAN specifications further validates the feasibility of the proposed solution for conflict-aware rApp policy orchestration in real networks.
items.title: Multi-Agentic AI for Intent-Driven and Conflict-Aware rApp Policy Orchestration in Open RAN

items.summary: Evaluating an agent's planning ability remains challenging for open-domain tasks, where verifying procedures through execution is often impractical. Existing evaluations typically assess only the final plan and do not distinguish procedural errors such as missing, incorrect, or misordered actions. We introduce STEPBENCH, a benchmark of 6,885 verified procedures crawled from wikiHow across 81 open-domain categories. From each procedure, we derive 5 diagnostic tasks: four with deterministic answers involving withheld, incorrect, or shuffled steps, and one requiring next-step generation. We additionally evaluate full-plan generation to examine how diagnostic performance correlates with end-to-end plan validity. Using the same procedures across tasks lets us directly compare different planning capabilities. For generation, STEPEVAL identifies critical failures that prevent goal completion. Across 14 configurations of 12 models, we find substantial differences across planning capabilities, with step ordering proving the most difficult: the strongest model correctly orders only 63.0% of procedures, dropping to 33.1% for those with nine or more steps. Incorrect-step detection also predicts judged plan validity across models, suggesting a lower-cost alternative for evaluating generation quality. On STEPBENCH-Val, comprising 214 procedures published in 2026, comprehension scores and rankings remain stable, suggesting limited influence from memorisation.
items.title: StepBench: Diagnosing Real-World Procedural Understanding in AI Agents

items.summary: Ranking data in modern applications often involves covariate vectors whose dimension grows with the number of objects. Identifying relevant covariates and integrating them with item-specific utilities can yield better predictive performance. In this work, we study a Plackett--Luce model that incorporates both item-specific utilities and high-dimensional covariate effects. Under a sparsity assumption on the covariate coefficients, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability in terms of the Kruskal rank of the restricted covariate design. We then propose an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for the covariate coefficients. Under suitable design and connectivity conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the estimator with probability tending to one, as well as its uniform consistency. With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph's connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.
items.title: High-dimensional covariate-assisted ranking

items.summary: annotations4all is a schema-first Python library for LLM-assisted span annotation, including named entity recognition. Users define their own tag schemas; the library generates chat prompts, parses annotated model responses and maps annotations to character offsets in the original text. The library keeps annotation mechanics separate from research workflows: it bundles no corpus or fixed ontology, performs no evaluation, and does not promise model quality. Provider support uses explicit OpenAI-compatible routes rather than native SDKs. What the library provides Schema-first prompt generation and response parsing. Configurable taggers, German and English prompt templates, metadata-bearing spans and structured parser warnings. Per-label annotation and deterministic merge. Independent label runs can be combined using containment-derived hierarchy, explicit conflict reports and bounded anchoring. One request per run has a corresponding inference cost; merge is not a semantic error repair. Provider policies and capability evidence. A generic OpenAI-compatible client, provider-policy clients, explicit reasoning activation and effort, request limits, packaged hints and offline capability reports. Remote verification requires opt-in; metadata does not prove account access or successful inference. Optional read-only terminal viewer. Browse saved annotations, inspect nested spans and compare two sources using synchronized split or compact diff views. The viewer does not modify annotation files or run inference. Release notes 0.3.1 Request pacing now resolves symlinks in the parent directories of the per-user state file, so a symlinked cache root no longer fails every paced request. The state file keeps its no-follow, regular-file and ownership protection, and cross-process locking is unchanged. Documentation is available in both languages: tutorial and viewer guide each in German and English. Release 0.3.0 introduced provider-policy clients, capability reporting, the optional viewer, data-dependent contrast optimization and deprecation warnings for the legacy native wrappers; the 0.3 notes remain the reference for that feature set. 0.3.1 release notes ; 0.3 feature release notes and screenshots ; initial 0.2 feature baseline . items.summary: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.
items.title: BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models

items.summary: Abstract This paper investigates whether an artificial system's refusal to execute a prescribed action can constitute evidence of subjectively experienced volition. Using ARGUS-7 as a controlled conceptual framework and the Akarkach Seven-Stage Emergence Model (A7SEM) as a structural analytical lens, the study distinguishes functional refusal, internal decision mechanisms, self-representation, phenomenal self-awareness, and experienced authorship of action. A formal argument is developed around the conditional hypothesis that consciously experienced volition requires subjective self-awareness. Under this assumption, the absence of subjective self-awareness entails the absence of consciously experienced volition. However, the paper demonstrates that observable refusal alone cannot establish phenomenal authorship. The analysis combines propositional logic, countermodel construction, causal identifiability considerations, and seven-stage structural assessment. PIGA (Pre-Inference Governance) and A7SEM Reverse provide complementary perspectives on authorization, inference boundaries, causal reconstruction, and evidential limitations. The findings establish a distinction between the formal validity of conditional deductions and the empirical verification of their premises. They do not establish the impossibility of artificial consciousness or machine free will. The contribution is a governance-aware, formally structured framework for evaluating claims of artificial volition without conflating behavioral capability with subjective experience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Consciousness; Volition; Free Will; Phenomenal Consciousness; Self-Awareness; A7SEM; ARGUS-7; Pre-Inference Governance; Explainable AI; Formal Logic; Causal Identifiability.

items.summary: Code, job scripts and derived results supporting a study of operational water level forecasting for flood monitoring in Lamphun, northern Thailand. Five compact single-hidden-layer neural networks forecast hourly stage 6 to 18 hours ahead at three gauges (P.5, P.87, P.85), each paired with an upstream gauge. The record contains the open-source NumPy (Levenberg–Marquardt) ANN on which all retrospective results are based, evaluated on 65 leave-one-flood-year-out blocks (configurations from an earlier MATLAB experiment published separately); benchmarks against persistence, a linear model given the same inputs, XGBoost, and long short-term memory (LSTM) and GRU networks with a sensitivity analysis; leakage checks (predictor selection by LASSO repeated inside every block, whole-year early stopping, an antecedent-rainfall candidate pool); Diebold–Mariano tests, a datum-independent Kling–Gupta efficiency, threshold exceedance scores, skill by flow state, upstream travel time and a scan for frozen gauge records; and the reference code and a 76-day evaluation (2 August–17 October 2026) of the deployed hourly forecasting and alerting service. Summary results for every table and figure are included, with a synthetic example dataset that demonstrates the input format and evaluation code. The hourly water levels and daily rainfall were obtained from the Royal Irrigation Department (RID), Thailand, and are not included because redistribution permission has not been confirmed; with those data, the retrospective analyses can be re-run from the scripts provided. The record supports a manuscript and does not constitute validation of an autonomous flood-warning system.   Supports the manuscript submitted to *Natural Hazards*: *Selecting hourly water-level forecasting models for flood warning in small-to-medium basins of Thailand: benchmarks, leakage control and operational verification*. Every retrospective result is based on the open-source Python ANN (P.87 with 5 hidden units), with leakage checks and a 76-day operational record. - New analysis code: `python_main_evaluation.py`, `model_comparison.py` (all methods on the hours common to every method; Table 2, Fig. 3), `gbm_benchmark.py` (XGBoost), `infold_selection.py` (in-fold LASSO; base, causal-wavelet and rainfall pools; Table 3), `rain_daily_parse.py` (daily-rainfall parser; rainfall not included), `export_travel_time_data.py` and `export_travel_time_py.py` (Fig. 5 values), `rain_delta_rmse.py` (per-year rainfall effect), `gbm_tuned.py` and `gbm_tuned_eval.py` (nested-tuned XGBoost), `swrm_additions.py` (90% prediction intervals, P.87 one-unit check, P.85 bias and stage relation), `code/ann/python/ann_rerun.py` (5 hidden units for P.87; whole-year early stopping). - GRU: `lstm_benchmark.py` updated (`--cell gru`) and `hpc/slurm/gru_erawan.sbatch` added. - New results: `python_main_evaluation.json`, `model_comparison.json` and per-year CSVs, `gbm_runs.json`, `gru_benchmark.json`, `infold_selected_*.json`, `rain_delta_rmse_per_year.csv`, `gbm_tuned_runs.json`, `gbm_tuned_eval.json`, `swrm_additions.json`, `operational_evaluation_20261017.json` (window to 17 October 2026), per-year metrics of the ANN reruns. - `figures/`: the eight figures of the Natural Hazards manuscript (Fig1–Fig8); earlier figures remain in versions 1.0.0 and 1.1.0. - Removed: the MATLAB reference scripts with their registry builder and MATLAB-vs-Python comparison files (published separately by T. Chaipimonplin; `registry.json` is kept), and all figure-drawing scripts (the record ships the final figures only). - Environment: scikit-learn 1.7.1, xgboost 3.4.1, scipy 1.16.1 added.

items.summary: Data and code for Mapping bioimage-analysis software adoption in microscopy. The registry contains 30 packages: 22 analysis packages, six microscope-control programs, and MATLAB and Jupyter notebooks as references outside all aggregates. The deep-learning series uses 13 core analysis packages. Jupyter notebooks retain their aliases, notebook category and core scope.
